newsitem.title: USA: State Department issues first environment report.
newsitem.headline: State Department issues first environment report.

text.p: The State Department on Tuesday issued its first annual report on the environment and said it was pursuing the fight against world ecological challenges on five fronts.

As part of a new "green" focus to U.S. foreign policy first announced last year, the report said "regional hubs" to promote environmental policies would be opened this year in U.S. embassies in six countries.

These are: Costa Rica, Uzbekistan, Ethiopia, Nepal, Jordan and Thailand. Six more hubs will be opened next year to help neighboring countries tackle problems specific to their regions, said the report, issued on Earth Day.

In a preface to the 32-page report, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said the administration was focusing on five problems -- climate change, toxic chemicals, species extinction, deforestation and marine degradation.
Both Albright and Vice-President Al Gore, who wrote a separate introduction, said environmental problems were now considered an integral part of U.S. national security.
Such problems "respect no border and threaten the health, prosperity and jobs of all Americans," Gore said.
"All the missiles and artillery in our arsenal will not be able to protect our people from rising sea levels, poisoned air, or foods laced with pesticides."

Albright said Soviet-era environmental disasters were impeding reform in Russia and central Europe, while population growth and competition for scarce resources were fueling "conflict and misery" in Central Africa.
Among statistics cited in the report were:
-- Seventy per cent of the world's marine fish stocks are "fully to over-exploited";
-- The people of the world annually release 23 billion tons of carbon dioxide into the air, raising the earth's temperature;
-- An estimated 70 species of living things are lost forever every day.
The report said no one country was responsible for the problems and only a cooperative approach would work.
The World Bank needed to factor environmental implications into its lending decisions, and the United Nations needed to be reformed to coordinate international action, it said.
